content.user_title: Apply and Troubleshoot PixiJS v8 Blend Modes
content.value_statement: PixiJS blend effects can fail because of missing extensions, renderer settings, or outdated APIs. This skill provides examples for correct setup, efficient ordering, and high-DPI troubleshooting.
actual_capabilities: Explain standard blend modes, including add, multiply, screen, erase, inherit, min, and max.
Show advanced blend extension imports and WebGL back buffer configuration.
Compare advanced blend modes by their documented visual effects.
Illustrate grouping adjacent objects by blend mode to reduce batch transitions.
Explain replacing PixiJS v7 runtime enum usage with v8 string values.
Troubleshoot high-DPI clipping using filter resolution inheritance and explain its resource costs.
limitations: Targets PixiJS v8 rather than providing a complete guide for older versions.
Provides documentation and examples, not an executable renderer, automated tests, or visual verification.
Advanced modes have filter overhead, and min and max require WebGL2 or later.
Batching examples are simplified; actual draw calls depend on other render state and scene constraints.

prompt_templates.scenario: Investigating rendering fidelity and performance together

output_examples.input: Why does color-burn look like normal blending in my WebGL scene?
output: Register the advanced blend modes extension before using color-burn.
Enable useBackBuffer when initializing the WebGL application.
Assign color-burn through the blendMode string property rather than a legacy runtime enum.

output_examples.input: My overlay effect clips on a high-DPI render target. What should I check?
output: Advanced blend modes use filters whose default resolution is 1.
Set filter default resolution to inherit before creating affected objects.
Higher filter resolution increases memory and runtime costs, so verify the result on your target renderer.

output_examples.input: My scene alternates screen and normal sprites. Can I reduce batch transitions?
output: Group compatible adjacent sprites by blend mode where visual stacking permits.
In the simplified example, grouping four sprites reduces blend-related draw calls from four to two.
Preserve overlap order and measure the actual scene because other rendering state can also split batches.

best_practices: Register advanced blend modes and enable the WebGL back buffer before relying on advanced effects.
Group compatible siblings by blend mode only when the visual stacking order remains correct.
Use inherited filter resolution when high-DPI fidelity requires it, and measure the memory and runtime impact.
anti_patterns: Using the PixiJS v7 BLEND_MODES runtime enum in v8 instead of string values.
Assuming advanced blend modes work without extension registration or the required WebGL back buffer.
Reordering overlapping sprites solely to reduce batch transitions without checking compositing correctness.

faq.question: Which PixiJS version does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It targets PixiJS v8 and explains differences from the v7 runtime blend mode enum.

faq.question: Which AI tools can use this skill?
faq.answer: The skill supports Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Do standard blend modes require the advanced extension?
faq.answer: No. Standard modes use built-in GPU blend equations. Advanced modes require the pixi.js/advanced-blend-modes import.

faq.question: Why can an advanced blend mode fall back in WebGL?
faq.answer: The extension must be registered, and useBackBuffer must be enabled during initialization. The skill notes that WebGPU enables the back buffer automatically.

faq.question: How can I reduce blend-related batch transitions?
faq.answer: Keep compatible siblings with the same blend mode adjacent when stacking order permits. Actual draw calls also depend on other rendering state.

faq.question: Does this skill run or visually verify my scene?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and TypeScript examples. You must run your application to verify appearance, compatibility, and performance.
